SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster malfunction thwarts double catch attempt
Science
Nov 13, 2026 7:20 PM EST
SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster malfunctioned and ended up in the water Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.
READ MORE: SpaceX's supersized Starship launches into orbit for the first time but flight ends early
Elon Musk's company had to lower its expectations when the first part of the double catch flopped.
Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster ended up in the Gulf of Mexico after an automatic abort. Despite the setback, the bullet-shaped spacecraft continued toward orbit. It will steer toward the pad Saturday for a similar grab, barring further trouble.
The Super Heavy v3 Booster 22 explodes upon being diverted to the water while retuning from the launch of a Starship 42 during the 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, Nov. 13, 2026. Photo by Joe Skipper/Reuters
It's the first time that the spacecraft will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. If all goes well, the flight will last 22 hours.
The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.
Grow your mind
Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the
wide worlds of science, health and technology.
Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship prepared to deliver 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.
The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.
SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is "how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000," SpaceX's Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida's Kennedy Space Center.
SpaceX's smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.
Falcon rockets "are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we're going to catch both the first stage and second stage," Dontchev said.
NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk's Starship or Bezos' Blue Moon.
During next summer's Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.

What to know about Microsoft's outage and why it takes so long to restore email services
Science
Nov 13, 2026 6:33 PM EST
This article originally appeared on The Conversation.
The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.
Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is "continuing to see improvements in service availability" but that "some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery."
Despite decades of predictions about its decline, email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.
When most people think about cloud outages, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.
Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn't designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.
Old architecture
When a typical cloud service breaks, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.
Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized "store-and-forward" architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.
Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting "send." During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.
From the sender's perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn't answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.
Major highway crash
One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don't stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.
In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.
When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.
First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.
Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.
Long, bumpy road to recovery
Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn't just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.
And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

All flights in the air are accounted for, he said during a news conference, adding that the public has no reason to be afraid.

The FAA's ground stop order runs through at least 11 p.m. ET Friday.
The ground stop was being imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," according to the notice from the FAA.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue was affecting the regional air traffic control centers that direct planes between airports nationwide.
He said FAA technicians are investigating.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

U.S. wrongly withheld New York highway funds over immigrant licenses, appeals court rules
Politics
Nov 13, 2026 5:55 PM EST
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. Transportation Department wrongly decided to withhold nearly $74 million in highway money from New York state after it refused to revoke nearly 33,000 questionable commercial driver's licenses for immigrants when an audit revealed problems last year, a federal appeals court said Friday.
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan concluded in a written decision that the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, an arm of the Transportation Department, acted in a manner that was "arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law" when it penalized New York.
WATCH: Duffy threatens to withhold millions in highway funds from New York over flaws in immigrant commercial driver's license system
The appeals court said the state can't be faulted for failing to cancel licenses when a commercial driver lost legal status to stay in the United States because rules that would require a cancellation were not in place at the time.
The driver's licenses pertain to commercial vehicles such as trucks, trailers, limousines and buses.
New York Attorney General Letitia James complained when the lawsuit was filed in April that the federal government was unfairly holding back money the state needs to repair roads and bridges. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring called the federal cuts "devastating" and characterized them as "political payback."
The Transportation Department said in a statement Friday that it makes no sense for states to let trucking licenses for foreign drivers stretch years beyond when they are legally in the U.S.
"We've put a stop to the madness to keep the driving public safe," the statement said.
The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers in the summer of 2025. Concerns about truck driver qualifications took on more urgency after an August 2025 crash in Florida, when a truck driver was accused of performing an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place.
Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant's work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying citizenship status.
Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally.
Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers while the non-domiciled licenses immigrants can receive represent about 5% of all commercial driver's licenses or about 200,000 drivers.
Immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted.
The dispute came after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy tightened rules governing when immigrants can obtain a commercial driver's license.
Officials said they took actions against states like New York after learning that some licenses remained valid long after an immigrant was no longer authorized to be in the country. New York issued licenses valid for eight years regardless of how long a driver's visa remained valid, authorities said.
A message seeking comment from the New York attorney general's office was not immediately returned.
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska.

FAA grounds all flights at U.S. airports due to air traffic control communications problems
Nation
Updated on Nov 13, 2026 7:06 PM EST — Published on
Nov 13, 2026 4:41 PM EST
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon for just the second time since the Sept. 11 attacks, with officials citing "extraordinary circumstances" caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances'
The nation's top homeland security official attributed the problem to a telecommunications outage and said there was no indication yet of a nefarious act. But the consequences were profound, disrupting potentially thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers who were heading home, expected as wedding guests or had other weekend plans.
"It's frustrating. This certainly sounds like it's going to be more than the usual run of the mill delay. I look forward to finding out why," said Jeff Dubner, a Washington, D.C., attorney, whose Alaska Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.
The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Friday's restrictions were imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," according to an FAA notice. The agency was investigating a communication issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
A few international flights were taking off Friday evening from international aviation hubs on the East and West coasts.
Top official says no sign yet of nefarious act
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that there was no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now."
"Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying," Mullin said.
WATCH: Homeland Security Secretary Mullin says FAA flight stoppage 'isn't another 9/11'
At least 600 flights have been diverted so far as a result of the FAA's order to ground all air traffic nationwide.
As of 5:50 p.m. Eastern, 496 flights were diverted to the airport from where they originally took off, while 104 were sent to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
Among the airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted are Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Denver International Airport, Dallas Fort Worth International Airport and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
An airplane prepares to land at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, , in Chicago, Illinois, Nov. 13, 2026. Photo by Jim Vondruska/Reuters
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, raising the likelihood of more cancelations and flight diversions.
At Chicago O'Hare Airport on Friday afternoon, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they gazed up at screens that showed flight delays across the board.
Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends, she said, had already arrived there.
"There's not really any information being passed to me," said the Seattle software engineer, who took a week of vacation for the trip. "I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I'm like, that would be miserable."
Austin Curtis and his wife were rethinking their trip from South Bend, Indiana, to a friend's baby shower in Denver after getting delayed during a layover in Chicago.
They had boarded a flight to Denver from O'Hare International Airport when they were told to get off the plane.
"We did see them taking luggage off our plane and others, so we're assuming it's going to be a pretty substantial delay," Curtis said.
They were unsure whether to get a hotel room or keep waiting out the delay at the airport. With care already in place for their two young children at home, they might stay the weekend in Chicago, he said.
"We might just make the most of it," Curtis said.
Despite the nationwide FAA ground stop, SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday afternoon on its latest test flight.
The government has been working to overhaul outdated technology
There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intellig

GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado loses U.S. House seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
Politics
Nov 13, 2026 4:32 PM EST
DENVER (AP) — Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert for a Colorado U.S. House seat on Friday, ousting a three-term Republican and staple of conservative media.
READ MORE: Democrats gather in Denver for post-midterms introspection-turned-celebration
Laubacher is a former Navy rear admiral. Her win in the 4th Congressional District race is just one of several surprising Republican losses in what's shaping up to be the most lopsided election in half a century.
Boebert embodied this decade's version of Republican politics. The telegenic owner of a gun-themed restaurant named "Shooters Grill" in the western Colorado town of Rifle, she catapulted to notoriety alongside President Donald Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

Once elected to Congress, she refused to pass through metal detectors at the U.S. Capitol and taunted Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of the "jihad squad." After barely surviving her first reelection campaign, Boebert moved across Colorado to a more Republican district.
Republicans carried the 4th District by more than 18 percentage points in 2024. But even that wasn't safe for her in this year's midterm elections.
Boebert acknowledged the widespread losses as she returned to the Capitol this week, saying, "We collectively failed."
"It's very clear," she said. "The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress."

Rescues operations underway in New Orleans after tanker hits river cruise boat
Nation
Nov 13, 2026 4:00 PM EST
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A tanker struck a New Orleans river cruise with 129 passengers on board on Friday, partially submerging the boat. Rescues were underway on the Mississippi River, officials say.
Authorities did not immediately release whether there were injuries or deaths.
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the paddlewheel cruise boat while it appeared to be docked. People were seen in the river in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the American Heritage listed further into the water.
The cruise ship is operated by American Cruise Lines.
Lt. Stephanie C. Norwood with New Orleans Emergency Medical Services said all agencies are responding to rescue efforts.
